results.title: Touch and pain
results.content: David Ginty and Patrik Ernfors are awarded The Brain Prize 2026 for pioneering work on the cellular architecture of somatosensation, revealing how the nervous system detects and processes stimuli such as touch and pain. Portrait photo David Ginty - The Brain Prize Winner 2026. Portrait photo Patrik Ernfors - The Brain Prize Winner 2026. The Brain Prize 2026 is awarded to Professors David Ginty and Patrik Ernfors for: Pioneering work on the cellular architecture of somatosensation, revealing how the nervous system detects and processes stimuli such as touch and pain. Patrik Ernfors and David Ginty transformed our knowledge by revealing the cellular building blocks of somatosensation and the neural principles by which they are organized. ## Cellular architectures of touch and pain: the twin contributions of David Ginty and Patrik Ernfors. Review article by Professor Fan Wang (MIT) tracing the evolution of somatosensory research and highlighting how the work of David Ginty and Patrik Ernfors have shaped our understanding of the cellular architecture underlying touch and pain.

results.content: # The world’s largest brain research prize awarded for groundbreaking discoveries on how we sense touch and pain. The Brain Prize 2026 is awarded to Professors David Ginty (US) and Patrik Ernfors (Sweden) for their pioneering discoveries on how the nervous system detects and processes touch and pain. Although touch and pain have been studied for more than 150 years, Patrik Ernfors (Karolinska Institute, Sweden) and David Ginty (Harvard Medical School, US) have revolutionised the field by identifying how nerve cells in the skin transform painful, thermal and mechanical stimulation, such as stroking, vibration, or indentation, into neural signals. The fundamental new insights into the neuroscience of touch and pain provided by Patrik Ernfors and David Ginty are truly remarkable and carry hope for patients living with disorders such as chronic pain. ### The world’s largest brain research prize awarded for groundbreaking discoveries on how we sense touch and pain.
